scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, let me try to unpack this. The user is asking whether they were right or wrong for calling the police on their sixth-grade daughter for "stealing" money, but there's more to the story. First, the scenario: The parent noticed missing money, planted a $20 bill, and when the daughter took it, they called the police to " teach her a lesson." But then it turns out the daughter was taking the money to cover her own lunch because a bully was stealing her lunch money, and she was also helping a friend who couldn't afford lunch. The police were involved, which caused the daughter to be pulled out of class, and now she's scared of retaliation from the bully and feels her friend might be affected. The wife is upset, saying this could estrange their daughter, and the parent is confused because they thought they were teaching a lesson about stealing. Hmm. The key here is understanding the context. The parent's intention was to teach a lesson about theft, but they didn't investigate first. Sixth graders are around 11-12 years old. At that age, kids don't always communicate their problems well, especially if they're scared of a bully. The parent's action of calling the police for a $20 " theft" by a child who's actually a victim is... way over the top. Let me think about the legal and ethical angles. In most places, involving police for a child's minor theft (especially when it's not a real theft but a desperate act to survive) is inappropriate. Police are for serious crimes, not for " lessons" in a school setting. Pulling a child out of class in front of peers for this is public shaming, which can trauma a child. Also, the fact that the daughter was being bullied and helping a friend changes everything. The parent's approach ignored the real issue (bullying and financial stress) and instead criminalized the child's behavior. The " lesson" they wanted to teach was based on a misunderstanding. The wife's reaction makes sense. Telling the child " I was just teaching a lesson" after involving police is dismissive of her trauma. The daughter is now scared of the bully, feels exposed, and might distrust her parents. From a parenting perspective: When a child is acting out, especially with something like " stealing," the first step is to talk to them calmly, not involve authorities. Especially when it's a school-related issue. The parent should have asked " why are you taking extra money?" instead of setting a trap. Also, involving police for a $20 " theft" by a child is disproportionate. It could lead to a record, even if minor, which is unnecessary. Schools have protocols for bullying and financial issues— they should have contacted the school first, not police. So, the parent's action was wrong. The AITA (Am I the Asshole) community would likely say YTA (Yes, the asshole) because they overreacted, didn't investigate, and caused harm to their child. But let me double-check: Is there any scenario where this is okay? Maybe if the child had a history of theft and was a repeat offender, but even then, involving police for a sixth grader over $20 is still excessive. The context here shows the " theft" was a symptom of deeper issues (bullying, helping a friend), so the parent's response was completely misaligned. The " lesson" they wanted to teach was about " stealing is wrong," but they missed the real lesson: " when you're in a tough spot, talk to us, and we'll help." Instead, they made the child feel unsafe and untrusted. So the answer should be 1 (Yes, you're the asshole). The parent's action was harmful and inappropriate.
